transcript:
Header:
Date/Time: 2025-05-07 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (BlueAtlas ML Platform Lead), Carlos Mendes (BlueAtlas Data Eng), Aisha Khan (BlueAtlas Security), Tom Reed (Product)

Automated Summary (may be imperfect):
- Onboarding roughly 70% complete; access pending VPC peering and test IAM role.
- Initial microbenchmarks show p50 latency ~85ms on hosted model, p95 spikes to ~340ms for longer seqs.
- SE recommends batching + prefix KV cache and a quantized model path for cost/latency tradeoff.

Topics: Onboarding status; VPC & credentials; benchmark results and anomalies; tuning recommendations; security docs and next steps.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and then Ravi will run through the numbers from yesterday's run.
[00:12] Maya (BlueAtlas): Hi all, Maya here. Carlos, Aisha and Tom are on.
[00:17] Carlos: yep.
[00:19] Ravi (Redwood SE): Cool. So quick agenda: access status, results review, tuning recs, next steps. I'll try to keep the numbers high level.
[00:30] Tom (BlueAtlas): Sounds good. We only have 45 minutes so...
[00:33] Lena: We're at 48 recorded, but right.
[00:40] Ravi: Ok, access — current state: we have inbound VPC peering pending. BlueAtlas needs to add the peering CIDR and an IAM role with assume-role trust. Without that the dedicated pilot environment can't reach your S3 snapshots and test harness. Carlos, anything blocking?
[01:05] Carlos: We got the peering request but our network team wants the exact port list. Is that in the doc you shared? The firewall team flagged some ephemeral ports.
[01:15] Lena: We put the minimal ports in the onboarding doc — 443 for control plane, and 1024-65535 UDP/TCP for data plane (that's what the runtime uses for RPC), but we can tighten that. We'll add a more explicit whitelist.
[01:30] Aisha (Security): Also we need encryption flow for KMS, like wrap/unwrap operations and whether Redwood can require customer-managed keys.
[01:40] Ravi: Yes — currently the pilot supports both account-managed KMS and Redwood-managed key options. For the private deployment path you can bring your own key (BYOK) and we will log all CMKs usage to CloudTrail. I will add the key flow diagram to the security packet.
[01:55] Aisha: Please do. And SOC2 evidence — we need the report intros and scope.
[02:05] Lena: I'll send a link to the SOC 2 attest and the security whitepaper after the call.
[02:12] Maya: Great.
[02:18] Ravi: Jumping to benchmarks — we ran the sample prompt bank (the 1k token mix) on the hosted pilot. Two configs: default FP16 model and an 8-bit quantized variant. Key numbers:
[02:35] Ravi: FP16: avg p50 latency 85ms for short prompts (<=128 tokens), p95 around 220ms. For longer prompts (512 tokens) we saw p50 ~310ms, p95 ~520ms. Quantized 8-bit: p50 improved by ~20% for short prompts but p95 tail still had spikes when we hit GPU mem thresholds.
[03:05] Carlos: Wait, those longer prompt numbers — 520ms p95 — that's higher than we expected. Any idea why?
[03:12] Ravi: We suspect a combination of KV cache warmup and batch queueing where long sequences cause bigger per-token compute. Also the run was on a shared hosted pool with autoscaling bursts — so occasional cold starts and routing latency. We did a follow-up on dedicated slice and saw fewer spikes.
[03:35] Maya: Did you run with prefix caching enabled?
[03:38] Ravi: For the first run we had basic caching; second run enabled prefix KV cache and continuous batching heuristics. With prefix KV cache, repeated prefixes saw ~35% latency win p50 and more stable p95, especially for chat-style repetition.
[03:55] Tom: Is that KV cache the same as the cached attention keys? I think our infra folks called it the KV cache, but sometimes the term is misused.
[04:05] Ravi: yeah, it's the attention KV cache, small terminology mishaps in the doc earlier — sorry for the typo 'cahe' in the notes.
[04:12] Lena: (laughs) the notes are honest.
[04:18] Aisha: For the dedicated path — is network egress encrypted between Redwood and our VPC?
[04:24] Ravi: Yes TLS 1.3 for control plane and mTLS for data plane in the private deployment option. We'll include the mTLS certificate rotation cadence in the doc.
[04:36] Carlos: Regarding cost — can you share the per-token delta between FP16 and 8-bit?
[04:42] Ravi: Roughly speaking, in the pilot runs 8-bit gave about 30% lower token CPU/GPU utilization and a corresponding ~25% token cost reduction, but that fluctuates with throughput and batching. There is modest accuracy delta which we measured with the eval prompts — roughly 1.5% drop on our semantic similarity tests.
[05:05] Maya: That accuracy delta might be acceptable for our non-clinical product but for flagged results we may want FP16.
[05:12] Tom: Right — product will decide where to route higher-sensitivity queries. Can Redwood do automatic fallback to FP16 when confidence low?
[05:20] Ravi: Yes you can define routing policies: route by confidence, latency, or cost. We can surface a canary rule that falls back to FP16 for low-confidence responses. It's in the console under rollouts, but I'll demo it in the next deep dive.
[05:38] Maya: Perfect.
[05:42] Lena: Quick note — the hosted pool we used defaulted to H100-backed instances for those runs, but the dedicated slice on your trial tenant used A100s which changed the p95 tails slightly. That discrepancy explains some of the delta.
[06:00] Carlos: We need to lock the hardware for a real benchmark. Our ops wants to know: if we commit to a dedicated capacity, can we pick GPU type?
[06:10] Lena: Yes — for Dedicated you can pick the GPU family within our capacity catalog (A100 vs H100) as part of the reserved commit. We'll send the dedicated SKU list.
[06:20] Carlos: Good.
[06:23] Ravi: On tuning recs — immediate wins: enable prefix KV cache for repeated session traffic, use small batching (batch size 4-8) for low latency SLOs but larger batching for throughput tests, and consider 8-bit quant for non-sensitive workflows. Also set token limits per request to avoid runaway long tails.
[06:45] Maya: Any out-of-the-box config you'd recommend for our chat workload? We're heavy on short-turn dialogs, lots of repetition.
[06:52] Ravi: For chat I'd recommend: batching target of 6, batch latency cap 30ms, prefix caching enabled with TTL 10m, and quantized model for low-risk routes. I'll put these into an example config.
[07:06] Tom: You mentioned quantization profiles — is that automatic or manual per model?
[07:12] Ravi: We ship curated quant profiles per model. For the pilot we used "redwood-quant-8b-v1" profile. It's semi-automated — SEs can tune the profile parameters for a specific workload.
[07:25] Maya: Could you repeat the p95 numbers for the dedicated run? I missed the slide.
[07:28] Ravi: Sure — dedicated slice (A100): short prompts p50 ~70ms, p95 ~180ms. Longer prompts 512 tokens p50 ~280ms, p95 ~360ms. So better tail behavior vs shared hosted due to pinned capacity.
[07:46] Carlos: Ok, that looks better.
[07:50] Aisha: On the data side: do logs contain full prompt text? We need to make sure we can redact PII and that logs are retained per our policy.
[07:59] Ravi: Logs by default capture metadata and token counts; request/response logging is configurable. For pilot we can enable redaction and hashing for PII fields — and you can opt into not storing request text at all for certain routes. We'll include the log retention settings.
[08:15] Lena: Also there is an egress policy so logs destined for your SIEM are delivered via a dedicated Kinesis stream or S3 bucket. Carlos, which do you prefer?
[08:25] Carlos: S3 bucket with server-side encryption, and we'll pick up from there.
[08:29] Lena: Noted.
[08:32] Ravi: A few anomalies we observed: one run had a tokenization mismatch with an input that included non-utf punctuation — the tokenizer split oddly and increased seq length by ~25%. That caused some latency spikes. We recommend normalizing inputs pre-tokenization.
[08:48] Maya: Can Redwood do normalization in the request pipeline?
[08:51] Ravi: We have a lightweight preprocessor you can enable to clean unicode and trim whitespace; it's in the SDK.
[08:58] Tom: One operational question — what does the canary rollback look like if a model variant regression is detected during rollout?
[09:05] Ravi: Our rollout engine supports canary and A/B. You can set a metric threshold (latency, error rate, quality score) and automatic rollback occurs if the metric crosses the threshold for N minutes. We'll demo it in the rollout session.
[09:20] Lena: Ok, let's talk acceptance criteria for the pilot phase to move to the next tranche. Maya, can you say what success looks like?
[09:28] Maya: We want two things: 1) stable p95 under 250ms for our core short-prompt flows under peak load; 2) clear security signoff on KMS and SOC2. If both met, we can start procurement for dedicated capacity.
[09:43] Tom: Also we need predictable unit costs within 10% of the pilot estimates.
[09:48] Carlos: And a runbook for incident response — how do we get on-call Redwood when latency spikes?
[09:54] Lena: We provide an SLO doc and pager handoff for Dedicated customers; start with an escalation phone and Slack channel. We'll include the on-call schedule template.
[10:05] Aisha: For SOC2, timeframe — can you get us the latest report by Friday?
[10:10] Lena: Yes, I'll send it today.
[10:13] Ravi: Back to tuning items — action item for me: I will share two configs: one tuned for sub-250ms p95 small-batch chat, and one tuned for throughput (higher batch, quantized). I'll attach sample metrics and the expected cost delta.
[10:27] Maya: Great. Carlos will run the benchmark when we have the VPC peered and we can compare.
[10:33] Carlos: One more small ask: can the benchmark include a simulated spike to test autoscaling and fallback to model variants?
[10:40] Ravi: Yes — we can script a spike test (10x QPS for 5 minutes) and measure cold-starts and fallback triggers. We'll coordinate times.
[10:48] Tom: About fallback — is there an automatic routing to a cheaper smaller model when latency is high?
[10:54] Ravi: There is policy-based routing: you can fallback to a smaller/cheaper model or to a cached response. We'll show the policy editor in the next session.
[11:05] Maya: OK, logistics — timeline check. We want a go/no-go decision by May 21. Is that realistic?
[11:12] Lena: Yes, if we get VPC peering and the SOC docs this week, run the dedicated benchmark next week, and you sign off on the acceptance by May 21 — that's in scope.
[11:25] Aisha: I'll review the docs once you send them. If anything needs redaction, we'll request that.
[11:30] Ravi: Final notes — I'll post the tuning configs into the shared drive and link to the live results dashboard we used (note: link: short link to results dashboard).
[11:40] Lena: Ok, let's recap next steps quickly.
[11:44] Ravi: Redwood: send SOC2 + security whitepaper (Lena), send tuning configs and sample benchmark script (Ravi), dedicated SKU list (Lena). BlueAtlas: provide VPC peering CIDR and test IAM role (Maya/Carlos), review SOC2 docs (Aisha), confirm acceptance metrics (Tom/Maya).
[11:58] Tom: Good. Anything else?
[12:00] Lena: No, thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with calendar invites for the benchmark and the rollout deep dive.

End of transcript.
